utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, my LiveNote is not functioning. But I now see a difference on my screen. I will just try to fix it. There is still no text on my LiveNote. Could someone assist me in fixing my LiveNote on my laptop. If there are no other issues to be addressed at this very moment, I would ask Madam Usher to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. DP17. May I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- That you have given at the beginning of your testimony. Having been examined by the parties, the Judges would have some questions for you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First is Judge Nieto-Navia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. You mentioned during your testimony some places in which according to your information the BH Army produced weapons and ammunition. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Might the witness be provided with map 1814. Do you see any of those places in that map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Would you please take a red pen, a red one, put a cross and a "W" in each of those places, "W1," "W2" et cetera and please give us the address or the street or the just for the -- for having that in the transcript. Which place is that, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the wire factory at Alipasin bridge, that would be the location. And before the war that was also the address of this factory. And in this part of the map, you can't see the technical school, it doesn't say Marijn Dvor, that is the central part of Sarajevo. It is the mechanical and technical school but I can't mark it because part of the map is missing. It is to the right of this map, the facility I am talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... To an arrow showing the place, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Similarly, the railway and industrial school is missing in Zivka Josila Street, that is where it was located and that would be here more or less if you can see it on the screen. It would be where my finger is, if we had the second start of the map. If you have the eastern part of Sarajevo, if you have a map of the eastern part of Sarajevo, it would be easier for me to be precise when answering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Are there other places on this map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The places that I had information about, no, they are not on this map. But they are in the eastern part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned if I am not wrong, four places in which the UNPROFOR or the UN military observers had posts. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Can we finish with this matter? I can repeat the sites where weapons were produced. I can repeat that, although I can't mark it on the map because part of the map is missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: It is not necessary.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not necessary, all right, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Another issue, the issue of UNPROFOR and the military observers posts. Do the same exercise, please, putting instead of the "W" a "UN" mark, "UN1," "UN2" et cetera.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Last time I forgot Energoinvest. There's something there too, so I will mark this too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I am sorry, Energoinvest was a weapon factory, was a UN post? What was that? I cannot see.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was an UN checkpoint, and on our part it was an observation point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you. So "UN2."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Is that "UN3"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These were all postwar names. These are all postwar names. These streets are not that familiar to me now. Very few names retained the prewar names that they had. That is why I am taking some time to locate the UN checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am unable to see where the witness wrote. Perhaps the ELMO could be adjusted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: The last one?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please point again at where you last have written something on the map.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the place I mentioned. And the Prosecution asked me whether this could be seen from the command, if you remember. That's in the Velika Aleja that goes towards Bosna, and in that part where the arrow is, our command was in front. And in front of that command in the direction of the lines there was the fourth checkpoint that I have marked. I don't know if I should mention that there was an UNPROFOR battalion which was located at the airport. And I don't know whether I should mark that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: No, no. I think that it is not necessary to do that. Thank you very much. No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions for you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] I would like to make sure that I have understood you correctly. When you drew the confrontation line on this map in the Nedzarici area, the line shows that Nedzarici was not entirely under the control of the Serbian forces. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in general, generally speaking, most of that area, apart from a few houses, in Nedzarici as can be seen on the map, most of the area was under the control of the Serbian forces. But the urban part of the Nedzarici area -- perhaps what is written here is confusing you. For us Nedzarici is this area that is marked here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, exactly, that's where it says Nedzarici. You marked the line there that -- it goes through the written word.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it would be more realistic if this word Nedzarici was written -- well, you can see where I am pointing to now. You can see it on the map. I don't know why it is being written here. It is a recent map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me. I just want to make sure that I have understood you correctly. Nedzarici wasn't entirely under your control. There was a part of Nedzarici that was under the control of the enemy side.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a very small area, an almost negligible area, because I would like to repeat that this map was made after the war. I don't know why the word Nedzarici is so far to the right. This is in fact Nedzarici, this part that I am pointing to now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you can confirm that the lines that you drew are the exact lines that correspond to the actual situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. My second question concerns --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Could I just clarify one other detail? You can see these buildings that are marked here, that's where Dobrinja V begins. Dobrinja V already begins in this part. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me to interrupt you. What I want to make sure of is that you drew the line in the area where you thought the confrontation line was; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move on to another subject, then, please. You stated that with regard to taking the Otes area, you explained this, I will quote you in English, you said [In English] "In one of the defence attacks, this part was liberated." [Interpretation] And you explained that this defensive attack took place in December 1992. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. My question then is: Did you state that there were buildings that had several floors which were used, as far as you know, by snipers who fired on your positions or fired at your population, and as a result you decided to organise what you called a defensive attack. My question consists of two parts: First of all, I'd like to know whether this area, the Otes area which was taken by your forces during the defensive attack was an inhabited area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to our information, there were very few civilians there, if that's what you are asking me about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because you said -- just a minute, please. Listen to my question and then answer it, please. You said that there were buildings that were used among others by snipers in order to fire at your population or at your posts, and you decided to launch a defensive attack, to plan a defensive attack, that's the term that you used. I simply want to know whether this area that you call Otes, I'd like to know whether there were any inhabitants there, was this an area where people lived or were there just snipers there? Were the buildings empty, apart from a few sniper nests? Were there any civilians who lived in this area; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't just have a few sniper nests there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I apologise, Judge, but there were not just a few sniper nests. There was the line, the entire line there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you know, in this -- just a minute, please. In the area that you call Otes, there were no civilians who lived in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. I didn't say that not at any time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In December 1992, please, when you launched your defensive attack, were there any civilians living in that area; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the buildings against which we launched defensive attack, there were no civilians there. There was just the line and quite a lot of Muslim troops, not just a few snipers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there were no civilians in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area where the line was, that's the area that I am talking about and the buildings that were part of the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The zone that against which you launched a defensive attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That means -- you mean to say there was civilians there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There weren't any civilians in the part against which we launched an attack. There were just Muslim forces there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The area called Otes that you aimed at --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Otes area is a far wider area, greater area than this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the zone that you mentioned, you pointed it out on the map, and you said that is this part was liberated -- just a minute, please. How can you answer without hearing my question? Wait for the question and then answer and I will listen to you attentively then. You said this area that you liberated, you were talking about an area, you were talking about a zone, but not just a few buildings. And I simply want to know whether there were any civilians in that zone, in that area; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yet again I am not just talking about a few buildings. I don't know whether the interpreters are interpreting this correctly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will move on to another subject. Were you familiar with the plan for the defensive attack, how did you carry out that attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally at the time was -- did not have such duties. My duties didn't involve me participating in that defensive attack at the time. But I was indirectly included in it, but I wasn't personally involved in it, so I can't really say yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Do you at least know which weapons were used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Which weapons were used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, mostly infantry weapons, as well as field guns, mortars, such weapons on the whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I have understood you correctly, mortars, that was to prepare the terrain in a certain sense. There were field guns, there were mortars and then an infantry attack, in accordance with the traditional rules?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the mortar attack and the field guns used, they were used against buildings, the buildings, in which the enemy side had its troops?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was directed at the enemy line from which they fired on us. We directed our attack against that line. Could you please try to understand that the front was a fairly -- a fairly wide area. It doesn't just consist of the few buildings that you have just mentioned. Because the line was several kilometres long, buildings can't cover that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have understood you correctly, this is an interesting point, because initially you said that you had liberated a zone. A zone is not just a line. It is an area, it has a depth.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Sir, let's move on to another subject, please. Answering a question that was asked of you, you answered, and I am going to quote you in English [In English] "You could hear the shell coming from the direction of Igman." [Interpretation] And you spoke of field gun firing. Now, my question is in relation to the sound. Were you able to determine the direction of fire based on the sound, and particularly, if these were mortars, you, who had the experience of a confrontation line, were you more or less able to hear the shell and to determine, more or less, the origin of fire? Because you said [In English] "The shell coming from the direction of Igman." [Interpretation] That is to say, if I understood you correctly, you were trying to say that according to the sound you were able to determine the origin, the source of fire.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But primarily based on the firing position, and I even commented on this, I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well. But I am talking about the possibility view. You have lived in this period of war, and you are able to, on the basis of a sound of a shell, to determine the source, the source of the fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I am repeating, that's not what I said. I was just speaking about the position of the firing. But the shell, when it is falling in the vicinity, and I think I said this, if the shell is going, flying over you 20 to 50 metres, then you hear it. But I commented what I said was that the soldiers have said that once you hear a shell, it's too late then, that's precisely what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you yourself, you personally, you cannot determine the source of firing on the basis of sound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the sound of the shell that's flying, you cannot hear it unless it is going, flying over you. But the firing position you were talking about, the locations, you were asking me a question, how was it possible to locate where the fire is coming from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. I am not talking about the sites, the firing sites. I am talking about a fly-over of a shell.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's very hard to answer that question. It's very hard. For instance, if you -- if you -- if a Maljutka is fired, then you hear this kind of hiss, and then if you hear that, you know that you have been fired on with a Maljutka. But with other projectiles, all kinds of field guns and calibres that were fired on us, it was impossible to determine, I was not able to determine which calibre was being fired on us. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You also said in relation to the stabilisers of a mortar shell falling on asphalt surface, you said that it was impossible that the stabiliser would be embedded, and that the only possibility was if something that could occur, that if the safety valve wasn't activated, wasn't taken out, taken off; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are my experiences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But, yes, yourself, did you observe -- did you observe a stabiliser embedded in the asphalt? Because "the security valve hadn't been activated"? Were you personally able to observe such an occurrence embedded in the asphalt?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly you asked me whether an unexploded shell, if I had seen such an unexploded shell embedded in the asphalt; is that what you are asking me? Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, have you ever seen an unexploded shell which was embedded in the asphalt, however?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you yourself, you are certain that the security of the safety valve hadn't been activated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's impossible -- you cannot establish this. You cannot determine this. Because there is a risk -- let me just clarify. There is a risk. For instance, if you mechanically going to take the shell out because you don't know why the shell hadn't exploded, perhaps you may try and go for it, reach it, get it out and then it might explode. Let me just explain, this shell has to be destroyed by explosive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, sir, but what you are saying, you yourself have seen shells embedded in the asphalt?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can tell you that, if you know Sarajevo, near Kula restaurant until a year ago, there was this kind of shell just next to the restaurant. There is a shell standing there and nobody dares to do anything about it. You have to destroy it with an explosive but if you do that, the whole restaurant would blow up, so there is this shell here. That's an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I am asking Mr. President to be patient, if you allow me another five minutes. You also spoke of a problem, and I am going to quote you so that I don't -- [In English] "And then as it is often the case, there would be unruly behaviour." [Interpretation] Was this phenomenon, this occurrence you are speaking -- I am quoting you in the context that you spoke about this issue -- you were speaking about your soldiers, the soldiers who were members of your brigade. And you said that that it happened, that some soldiers would drink alcohol and then their behaviour would be unbecoming to soldiers. So was this a phenomenon that was frequent? Do you know of several occurrences like this? Can you give us some examples, when you say "their behaviour," how did they act? What kind of behavior was that that they were exhibiting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't say quite like that, what you've quoted, Your Honour, the way you've taken it out of the context. I have spoken hypothetically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to interrupt you because I am going to quote you and I can give you the page. This is what you said [In English] "And then as it is often the case there would be unruly behaviour." [Interpretation] And that is perhaps a translation, but I am saying to you what is in the English transcript. So if you say that is not what I said, then I am all ears, listening to what you have to say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for your understanding. But that's not what I said. Then it is a very bad translation. I was speaking hypothetically when the Prosecutor was asking me what were the tasks, that was the context, what were the tasks, the duties of the Military Police. And personally my duties as security officer, so I said among other things, one of the tasks was to prevent such occurrences, possible -- probable occurrences. So, perhaps, if there is smuggling of alcohol, if there is this kind of trafficking in alcohol, so because if this allowed to sell alcohol, for alcohol to be consumed, then such situations, that was the context that I said this in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. I wasn't speaking about the trafficking. I am speaking only about alcohol. Very well. So I am coming to the end of my questions. Perhaps I have one or two more questions. You spoke -- you said that one day you were called to go to the observation post of the United Nations and if you wish, I'll quote you. You said [In English] "They wanted me to go to their observation post." [Interpretation] Do you recall the reason why or the occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall very well. The gentlemen who were at this observation post said that it would be with great difficulty that they would remain there at this post because the Muslims were constantly firing in spite of the warning to the Muslim command, they were firing at the observation post. And I went and I saw for myself there were 50 shots, more than 50 shots. They could have only come from the Muslim side. They came directly to the post, on to the post where the UN observers were. So these persons wanted to tell us, let us know why they were unable to remain at this post. And this part in Nedzarici towards Vojnicko Polje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did they change, did they actually change the post, the location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where did they go to? Did they go to a little further afield or where did they go to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. And I tell you why, because I was involved in other tasks. But this post, on this post, I didn't see them there any more. That was a protected post by bullet-proof glass, but if you can say that there were these traces, so to speak, scars, from -- from weapons being fired on the glass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Because what you have said on the map, you pointed exactly where they were posted, but I don't think that you then mentioned that they had changed the location. Very well. Let's go on to my last question. You said --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't ask me

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Just as well that I did ask you in the end. The very last question, sir, is in relation to something you said. You said that you -- that your brigade, that you didn't -- your brigade didn't have sniper rifles.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you said also [In English] "Weapons that could fire at a long distance." [Interpretation] So, as far as you know, the range of rifles used in your brigade went up to what distance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the rifles that we had at our disposal, theoretically speaking, and our instructions were that there is no point in using these for distances over 200 metres. Because these rifles were otherwise used for up to 400 metres, but these were -- these were not very precise rifles. And when we -- have to explain -- when we checked their ranges, when we tested them on the testing ground, very few people managed to hit a target at 100 metres with that rifle. So this is not a bad Serbian soldier shooting, but it's because the rifles were old and they were not good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the range of the rifle of the weapon, what is the range of that rifle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maximum range of this rifle, as far as I know, about 600 metres. But I am not completely sure. This is as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are speaking about all the rifles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I am speaking about the type of the rifle that was the most common rifle among our soldiers, that was AK-47 Kalashnikov rifle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I am speaking about rifles in general, rifles used by your brigade. Is that the only type of rifle that you had or were there any others that you had that had a longer range?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were also automatic rifles, M-56, and they had a shorter range in relation to the previous rifle. And then there was also the Browning gun that we spoke of. We had it and the Muslims had it too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, let's just focus on the rifles, please and different types of rifles. You said and you confirmed that your troops had only rifles with maximum range up to 600 metres -- up to 400 metres, is that what your testimony is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is when optimum conditions, when it is the best kind of rifle, when the barrel hasn't been damaged. Theoretically speaking, these rifles can shoot at a distance of up to 400 metres. You can also shoot at 500, and a kilometre, but they are not effective, they are not hitting the target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP17, I have got a few questions for you as well. Would you please not interrupt me when I put a question to you, and would you please listen carefully to the question so that you can answer it. You talked about an attack on Otes. You told us that mortars were used in this attack. From where were these mortars firing when they supported the attack on Otes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be perfectly honest, personally I didn't lead this operation. I am just saying this very sincerely, so I don't know exactly where from that they attacked. I wasn't even involved in this defensive attack as someone who established anything whatsoever. I carried out only -- what I mean is that if I knew it I wouldn't have a problem to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your answer is I don't know from where --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the answer to my question. How do you know that mortars were supporting this attack on Otes? Were you told that they were used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I was able to follow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was whether you were told. By whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see I answered yes, I said I knew. I could have just followed that over the radio, the radio link that we had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you know it from what you heard on the radio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My next question is: Were there any mortar crews in the School of Theology or Faculty of Theology?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There weren't. And practically that was impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I am not talking about mortars; I am talking about mortar crews. Your answer is still the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know that at the Faculty of Theology there were such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't know or do you know that there were not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I would have known had they been there. As far as I know, there weren't any there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You indicated -- and please could the witness be shown map 1814, D1814. You indicated where mortars were located. Could you please point at it again in Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us where the mortar crew was located that was responsible for those mortars? No, I am talking about the crew, yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, logically, yes, would be the closest to the area where the mortars were. This would be these houses in this part here. So this is what I am pointing to now. You can see it. That's where they were. That's where the crews were, the mortar crews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know or do you just assume that they were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that. I said that I saw that once, the mortars, and the fact is that they were able to move in case the enemy would locate them well and fire at them, it would be the most normal thing for them to move. But when I saw them, I know then that they were in a house next to where they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, let's now move to a mortar position you indicated at the opposite side of the line in Dobrinja. I think you indicated this by "15." Would you please point at it and could the map perhaps be moved a little bit, Madam Usher. Yes. Thank you. Could you please point again at where you located a mortar position in Dobrinja at the other side of the line.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's where you have written "15." What's the basis of your knowledge that a mortar was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: People who crossed over that went -- came to our side running across minefields, they gave us this information. That doesn't mean they were always there, but they told us, according to the information that we had at our disposal, they moved them as well in the same way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say it was a mobile mortar, and your knowledge is --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mortars can be used. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you not to interrupt me when I put a question to you. So you are telling us that it was a mobile mortar and the basis of your knowledge is what you've been told by one person or would it be more persons that came to your side of the line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: More persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know whether we have to turn into private session, but you gave a name during your testimony of one person. Could you -- do you remember the name of other persons who confirmed that a mortar was there. If you remember the name we could turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this moment, I can remember another name, apart from those that I have already given. Names and surnames.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We then turn for a moment in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session. Were there any M-48 rifles in your units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. If there were any initially, there were only very few because all soldiers had more confidence in these rifles that had more bullets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... Whether you were and you answered --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was there any difference in the presence of snipers in your battalion compared to other battalions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have any snipers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was whether there was any difference between your battalion and other battalions or would you say that it was the same in all battalions, that there would be no snipers in other battalions either?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am speaking about battalions in my brigade, so I want to make that clear. As far as I know, there weren't any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The -- do you know what unit was present at the Jewish cemetery? Am I right in understanding that the Jewish cemetery was not within your zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. It wasn't in our area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the presence of your troops near to the Jewish cemetery?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very little. I know there was frequent fighting. The radio and TV reported on this. But I know very little on this. Specifically I don't know anything because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So if you don't know anything, I won't put any additional questions to you. About shells coming from Igman, you testified that shells were coming from Igman and answering questions of Judge El Mahdi you said that not by sound you could identify them as coming from Igman; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's what I wanted to clarify. The Judge wanted to know whether the calibre could be determined. I asked whether it was a matter of the origin of fire, and I was told that it wasn't the origin of fire, but whether the calibre could be determined on the basis of the sound. I explained this, I wasn't in a position to do so, and I don't think anything else could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you listen carefully, I don't think the questions were about the calibre, but the source of fire of the shells --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please let me put the question to you. When you told us about shells coming from the direction of Igman, on the basis of what exactly would you be sure that they came from the Igman direction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was in the evening, on the basis of the flash and the noise you could hear, the explosion from the place it was fired from, and the flash, that was obvious. But observers observed the entire zone, and if there were several of them -- if several of them say that they saw something in such-and-such a part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... And a noise, as I understand you. And that was --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the explosion that you hear when the shell explodes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now during the day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of day, of the day, either visually, if it could be seen, but usually we would determine this on the basis of the explosion you could hear when a shell was fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now your personal knowledge when you yourself identified during this time that a shell was coming from Igman, when you did not see anything but when you heard the explosion, were you then able to identify on the basis of this explosion that it would come from -- that it was fired from Igman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. If I only heard the explosion and nothing else, that's how it was interpreted to me; is that your question? Well, yes, my answer is, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So just on the basis of the sound of the explosion where you didn't see a shell being fired, you were able to identify that it came from Igman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because one had the opportunity to hear it nearby. You develop a sense of hearing, not just me, but everyone who follows this. So you can tell whether something was fired from a kilometre or from two kilometres. It was possible to determine where the origin of fire was, more or less, not with great precision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So not only the direction, but also the distance, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, usually, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can be wrong. You can't be very precise in such situations. It depends on the weather, it depends on where you are. There are quite a few influences that factor this. And Igman covers a wide area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your answer. A next question would be: You told us that you would hear a shell fly just prior to landing; is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise again. But if you are near -- yes, but there are shells that you don't hear at all. But if we are talking about the shells when you are the target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is that because if the distance that you would not hear a shell flying over that would land somewhere else? Is that because of the distance between the man on the ground and the shell flying over high that you would not hear it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. The distance and in any case you usually don't hear it when it is flying over. I didn't have the opportunity of hearing a shell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have no further questions for you. Have the parties any need to put additional questions to the witness? Then, Mr. DP17, this concludes your testimony in this court. I know that you had to wait for quite a while. I also noticed that you had to come back twice. I appreciate your patience. I thank you for having answered the questions of both parties and the Chamber, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank you too, and I apologise if -- well, this is the first time that I have appeared before a court. So if I made certain attempts, this was just a matter of showing goodwill towards the Judges. And it was an honour for me to testify here. I don't know whether this is customary. I would just like to say hello to the General, to greet the General without any comments, without making any comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you've said it already. It is not usual, and it is usually not what we do in this court. But from his face, I see that he received some greetings from you. Thank you very much. Could you please, Madam Usher, escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, I hope you work continue with success and I wish all the best to the General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please guide us through the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, may I have some guidance as to whether you intend to tender both maps D1813 and D1814?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D1 -- I don't think the witness finished with D1813, it is D1814.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that would be sufficient for the Defence, then I take it D1813 is not tendered and D1814 is tendered. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D1812, under seal, pseudonym sheet; D1814, map marked by witness; D1312, B/C/S report dated 13/12/1992; D1312.1, English translation; D1313, B/C/S report dated 14/12/1992; D1313.1, English translation; D348/4 under seal, video in B/C/S; D348/4.1, under seal, English translation of D348/4; P2754 under seal, UNMO report; and P2759, UNMO report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in relation to P2754, it doesn't need to be tendered under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The testimony given in respect to that document was given in private session, but if the Prosecution who classified the document as an "R" document does not insist on admission under seal and if the Defence would agree that although the testimony was given in private session, there is no need to admit this document under seal. We could admit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have these two documents P2757 and P2759 and my objection to having these documents included is that the witness wasn't able to recognise these documents and was not in a position to confirm the coordinates. I think that you will take this into consideration when admitting the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, any --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Just this observation, Mr. President, that in relation to the witness not identifying the document, there was no basis for the witness to identify the document, but the Trial Chamber has already heard evidence in relation to the document P2754 from a witness who was in a central position in respect of the normal production of such documents. Mr. President, in relation to the map references, when read in conjunction with P2759 on the face of the document one of the positions is identified as the Home for the Blind. You will note that the same map reference is given in both. In relation to the second map reference, the Prosecution will seek to call evidence in reply to establish that that position is in fact as was put to the witness, approximately 10 metres from the intersection that was indicated to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace you are telling us that the testimony was given on 2754 by another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the other hand, no discussion has at that moment been taken about the admission into evidence of that document and you say if that witness recognise the document or the type of document we are talking about, we will have to consider whether when you did not tender that document, whether we could later rely on testimony in respect of a document which at that time was not tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, you may recall that at that stage of the Prosecution case, as a matter of course, the Prosecution often did not tender large numbers of documents that were shown to the witness in order to simply to avoid unnecessary paperwork. Instead, and as was done with this particular document, the witness's attention was drawn to this particular passage and it was read to him, and in that sense, even if the Trial Chamber did not admit into evidence the actual document in respect of that witness's evidence, his evidence would stand alone without the document. And it is sufficiently in evidence for it to be joined to this document now, because the relevant passage was read to him word for word, and he confirmed that it was correctly read to him and that the document was produced the normal way, and that he would have seen it at the time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will consider whether or not to admit 2754, and 2759 for which the same is true, I think, whether there is sufficient basis to admit it into evidence. The other documents are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When we consider whether there would be a sufficient basis to tender these documents into evidence, we have a provisional translation of one of these documents in B/C/S. I noticed that the translation given by the interpreters was not literally the same. Mr. Ierace, could -- while we are considering whether to admit this document or not, could the Prosecution perhaps check and perhaps the Defence is invited to do the same, whether this would be a translation that could serve to assist the Chamber in understanding -- no, not assist the Chamber, but whether this would be a translation which is similar enough to what has been read to the Defence and especially to the accused to be admitted into evidence. And when the accused has been informed on the basis of the translation given by the translators in this courtroom, if at any stage of the proceedings we have to check whether what has been read to the accused is, as far as the content is concerned, similar to what the translation says on paper. I would like to avoid that we have an oral translation which differs too much from the written translation that is admitted. If you seek to admit the -- you do not seek --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't seek to admit into evidence, that is to tender, the rough translation that was provided to the Defence. It was a, as the title indicates, a translation not prepared by an official interpreter, and if there is any discrepancy, then the interpretation provided by the court interpreters who are properly fully qualified should be relied upon. It was provided simply to assist the Defence to understand the contents of the document at short notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the translation as it has been given orally at trial is, in the view of the Prosecution, the content of that document. So we rely on that, if necessary, for the future. Then we will consider the matter. Is at -- we are now at a point where Witness DP51 could be recalled in order to be cross-examined. What would be wise? To do it right away? Let me just confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order not to unnecessarily interrupt the cross-examination, we will have a break now until five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution ready to cross-examine Witness DP51? Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness DP51.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are glad to see that you came back in order to be cross-examined by the Prosecution. May I remind you, although it is already quite some time ago, that at the beginning of your testimony you have given a solemn declaration that you would speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth, and that you are still bound by that solemn declaration while now continuing to give evidence in this court. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May the witness be shown the document which was shown to him before the adjournment. We have the translation, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, do you have the numbers available.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: We have translations on the document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I am merely going to show the document, Mr. President. It is not an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are just going to show it, you are not going to tender it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, you were shown this document on the previous date at the point of adjournment.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you please read out the title of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Serbian council of the Serbian Democratic Party. Information on the policies in Bosnia-Herzegovina, on health policies in Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you please read out the name of the person who has signed the document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professor Milutin Najdanovic, the late, he is an acquaintance of mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What is his designation as indicated on his document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the multi-party policies were implemented in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were five parties in power. Three national parties, one called the reformist party, the representative was a Croat. And the fifth one --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. Could you just give out the designation as indicated on this document, due to time constraints.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Coordinator of the commission for health of the SDS, Professor Milutin Najdanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, on the previous date having examined this document, you explained and if I may read out your own words, the transcript page number 13660, you explained, I will use your own words: "Once the multi-party came into existence in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that was in 19 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel slow down while reading, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: "Once the multi-party system came into existence in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that was in 1990, the political parties propose members of their own nation to become members of certain structures that were in charge of health care in Bosnia-Herzegovina." In using the term "political parties proposed members of their own nation" sir, did you mean members of their own political parties; is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They proposed members of their own nation and there was the -- there weren't the reformist and Yugoslav parties. A Muslim was in charge of the reformists, and some of the people here were in some of those parties. I can, I'll repeat that. When multi-party policies were introduced, the national parties proposed members of their own nation, people, not of their own party, specialists, prominent specialists who were capable of assuming certain duties concerning running the health system in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were also members from parties that were not national parties from the reformist party and the Yugoslav party. This person was in the Yugoslav party.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, your name is in the document, isn't it? Your name has been proposed as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did I hear the interpreters ask for the repetition of a name or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the interpreter did not hear the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under number seven, there is the name Zorica Vujisic, Dr. Zorica Vujisic. She was a member of the Yugoslav party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And your name has been nominated in place of number two, isn't that the case, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Document may be returned, may the witness be shown a map marked D1758.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The map has been admitted under seal, but it is not clear in my recollection for what reason. But it could be...

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It is possibly because the map indicates his area of his residence and his workplace, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we turn into private session and deal with the map in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, you testified that you saw an artillery school of the BH Army located at the Faculty of Architecture.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is in addition to the three tanks you claim to see in the very same compound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the tanks around the buildings. They don't enter the buildings and the school. I saw in the building, and I spent some time there too, about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So this school, artillery school, that you saw at the Faculty of Architecture as well as the three tanks should be visible from the -- from the route which go alongside the compound in which the faculties and the three tanks you claim to see was situated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't able to see the school from the building. I went into the building and saw the school. But the tanks could be seen from the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Weren't this road used regularly by UN personnel, including members of the UNPROFOR as well as UN monitoring observers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't look at them very often, because it was a narrow road and they used wider roads to go around in their vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Both roads alongside, whether it is wider or narrow, both roads go alongside this compound on either side; isn't that the case, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is one road, Hasana Brkica Road on one side, and behind the complex, the Kosevo complex, there is a narrow road, it's the Ivan Tomic road.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, have you seen UN personnel at the Kosevo Hospital? Have you seen the persons in the blue berets and the blue helmets at the Kosevo Hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw General Rose and I saw a Swiss doctor, her name was, I think -- I can't remember, but she came to see me personally on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you knew --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was a representative of the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you did know members of the UN, as well as members of the -- including members of the UNPROFOR who visited the hospital, you knew them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what was UNPROFOR and what the other structures were, but I could come across them in the town and within the complex of the Kosevo Hospital. But I couldn't distinguish between the two.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that UN personnel visited the hospital practically daily?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was not the case while I was working there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Wasn't there a generator provided to the hospital by the UN, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it would work for half a year. They even brought fuel for it, but that was not done on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Wasn't the refueling of the generator and the maintenance of the generator done by the UN?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that's not done every day, but when necessary, and sometimes that's in 15 days' time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, would you at least agree that the hospital complex was regularly visited by UN personnel, if not daily?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. They sometimes came to visit the hospital. I couldn't say what the intervals were, but they really did come occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to speak to any of them? You mentioned the name of General Rose. Did you have an opportunity to speak to -- have a conversation with one of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was in the corridor when he passed by. There is one thing that you have to understand, I was a Serbian and the foreigners didn't have to come and see me, only the International Red Cross came to see me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you have any problems about speaking to UN personnel or contacting them in any way? Did you personally have a problem? Or did you feel you had a problem?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, the people who took them around the hospitals were Bosniaks. They didn't bring them to Serbs. Only on two occasions did they come to see me personally. They went to a different office, and it was the representative of the International Red Cross, who was a doctor from Switzerland. She was the only person who came to see me personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, I don't mention your position because we are in open session, but considering the position you held, did it not occur to you to complain to the UN personnel or perhaps the member of the Red Cross who came to visit you to -- about the three tanks which are located in the adjoining compound or the artillery school which was located at the Faculty of Architecture?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, they were able to see that just like I was, but I didn't speak to them and I wasn't able to tell them about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So as you say you -- you are aware that they themselves saw this, the three tanks, you came to have seen and the faculty of -- the school which was located at the Faculty of Architecture? You just said they could themselves see it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to understand one thing: Whenever the international forces were in the vicinity the army took no action, but when they left, the army went into action. That was -- those were the tactics employed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, apart from UN personnel, did you ever see journalists come into the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On several occasions journalists did come, particularly after larger scale operations when there were more injured persons and following them, there would be journalists coming, very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you ever have the opportunity to speak to any one of these journalists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only spoke once with, I think his name was John Brown, an American reporter. In fact a doctor had linked us up with the request that he take me out of Sarajevo. Unfortunately he left three days later, and I remained.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When did you speak to John Brown, sir, the person -- the journalist named John Brown, when was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the summer of 1993, probably May.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you inform him of the three tanks you saw in the adjoining compound or the artillery school you claim to have seen at the Faculty of Architecture?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only spoke about my request that I be taken out of Sarajevo at that time or at that moment I wasn't interested in tanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So, is it your impression that you were not interested in bringing to a journalist's attention the fact that there was an element which posed a risk to the hospital just adjoining the hospital complex, even though you had the opportunity, is it your impression, and you were only interested in being taken out of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. Because any word that I would have spoken at that time in that context would have represented an additional risk for me. Don't forget that I was persecuted in the lift and the only thing that saved me was that a nurse took me up to the -- up all the way up with the elevator, and she saved me from being killed. And of course in such circumstances, a fear develops and along with it, the wish to leave this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, are you saying that you lived in fear during your stay in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived in fear -- I lived in an atmosphere of fear which occasionally became fear.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you did live in an atmosphere of fear, and you wanted to get out of it or remove yourself from that situation of fear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did your family live with you in Sarajevo during the period you worked and lived in Sarajevo, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The children did not. They were in Novi Sad in Yugoslavia, and my wife in the summer of 1993, I think it was June, she also went out and went to be with the children and I remained by myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So why did your children and the wife leave Sarajevo? Were you -- is it that you were scared for their lives and you asked them to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I feared -- I was in fear for their lives and I thought it was better that they -- for them to be elsewhere. You see, 200.000 people left Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So apart from yourself, sir, there were others, the civilians who too lived in fear, like you, sir, during this period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. They lived in -- with a certain amount of fear, with a certain amount of danger, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In your examination-in-chief, sir, you stated that you did not observe fear amongst the population, and let me quote you. Transcript is now page 13651. Let me quote you, sir. "However, I was not able to see some unusual behaviour among the population that would not correspond the situation around us. A person who is afraid has an improper reaction to the situation which one finds himself. This is what we call panic, and I did not observe panic. The hospital continued to operate as did schools although they schedule was somewhat different. But still they continued to operate. People even went to bars and restaurants and got married." You indicated, sir, in testifying in examination-in-chief that life seemed to proceed quite normally, yet now you do admit that people lived under fear.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reiterate what I said, everybody felt a certain dose of fear, but they were not living in panic, that is a different thing, although I am not a psychiatrist, but panic in my opinion means that that would be behaviour inadequate or not for the circumstances the person was living in. But if a person is worrying, is concerned that something unpleasant will happen, then that is a dose of fear, of worry. I lived with a little dose of fear. You cannot live in a state of panic. You cannot work in a state of panic, but you can live and work with a certain dose of fear, and that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, your testimony was that you left Sarajevo in January 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: After your release, after the arrest, sir, you did not go back to Sarajevo and you lived elsewhere, isn't that the case, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: During -- after you left Sarajevo, sir, where did you live or where did you work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived in the Serbian Sarajevo and after the war finished and since the war has finished, I have been living in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So when you lived in the Serbian Sarajevo as you put it, was there any risk or any threat to you or were you free to do as you please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't live freely. I didn't like to live there, but I didn't have any other conditions to live in. I was in the hospital, I lived in the hospital throughout this time. I was in a ward, in a medical hospital ward by myself, but it was a hospital ward.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: During this period, sir, did you not have the opportunity to inform the UN personnel of the three tanks you observed in the adjoining compound of the Kosevo Hospital or about the artillery school at the Faculty of Architecture which you claim to have seen? And I am saying after you left Sarajevo, after your arrest and you were living in the Serbian Sarajevo. Did you not have the opportunity or did you not think it proper to inform the UN?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all believed that they knew this, and that they had seen it, and that any additional information would have been superfluous or useless.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You did not think it appropriate to take that additional step to inform, in case it has not been observed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't think in this way. They could have read it in the press, published in the Serbian Sarajevo, and I believe that I have read this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Which press --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne apart from the next question which I will allow you to put to the witness, but would the nonreporting of three things not be a subject sufficiently dealt with until now?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I will just ask one more question with regard to that and move on. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You referred to the press in which people could have read about the tanks. Which newspaper or which media are you referring to, sir? Could you specifically mention the name of the newspaper, if it was a newspaper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am speaking about the television of Serbian Sarajevo, and I am speaking about newspaper a Serbian Oslobodjenje.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, during the time you worked in Kosevo, did you ever go out of the hospital complex to treat patients, if I may use the term, did you ever make "house calls"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't make house calls ever, and only on one occasion a deputy director for economic matters of the Kosevo Hospital in 1993 took me to operate on her sister in the city hospital. That is my only trip when I went to that hospital, the only time that I went out of the Kosevo Hospital and performed my duty as a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So that was the only time you left the Kosevo Hospital complex to treat any patients?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, in the examination-in-chief you stated that you went to the dental faculty to treat the wife of Juka Prazina whose headquarters you claimed was situated at the dental faculty near the Kosevo Hospital. So by your -- by what you just stated in your previous testimony that you left the hospital to treat Juka Prazina at the dental faculty is completely incorrect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dental clinic is very near behind the Kosevo Hospital. I went in my medical doctor's coat. I believe that that was within the Kosevo Hospital complex. That's why I said I went to see Juka Prazina's wife. But the other city hospital is in the other part of town. Because up to the dental clinic we were just all walking normally as if we were anywhere in the Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see the clock. I could perhaps come to a convenient point and stop or perhaps we could stop at this time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you still need, Ms. Mahindaratne

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: About another half hour, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Another half hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I believe -- yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you give me one second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'd like to ask you if I can finish tonight. I have duties elsewhere and just like last time, I am asking you, requesting to finish tonight. I have asked last time to be here just for two days and I have been here now six days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will do our utmost best. That's what I can promise you. In your interest and the interest of the Tribunal and of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I just come to a convenient point and then take the break

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you can do that in not more than a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, perhaps we could take the break at this time because I would need to show him the map to proceed. That would take some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, on the basis of the bookkeeping of the Chamber, there is 24 minutes left, and cross-examination as it went on until now, gives no reason for the Chamber to grant any more time than these 24 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the witness be shown map marked number D1758. Mr. President, maybe we have to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are now in open session and could you please proceed and could you please wait until the cursor stops moving.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir do you remember an incident where the abdominal surgery clinic was shelled in the last week of November 1993, and where two nurses were killed, are you aware of this incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about the shelling, but I didn't hear about the deaths. And I think that this is an incorrect information.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is it your impression, sir, that you never heard that the abdominal surgery clinic was shelled and two nurses were killed while three doctors and a technician were injured, is it your impression that you never heard of this or never learnt or this which was given much publicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about the shelling of the clinic for abdominal surgery but I am categorically saying that nobody was killed. It is one compound of one hospital, that is 100, 200 metres from where I worked and I would have know. And I knew all the doctors in that clinic. I would have to heard about somebody getting killed. After all I was a medical director and this information could have come to me in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Apart from the doctors, did you also know nurses who were working or attached to the Kosevo Hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know all the junior doctors of the Kosevo Hospital. There were 3.000 doctors and nurses, so no one doctor, no one person would have known every single doctor or nurse.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, did you know a nurse by the name of Heco Sefika?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I withdraw that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, have you visited the Kosevo Hospital complex since the cessation of hostilities, perhaps recently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Last year I went to the orthopaedic clinic with my friends. They were students of mine, or assistants, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Have you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were very well received.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: On that visit or perhaps before, have you observed or have you seen the memorial erected in the hospital premises in memory of the employees of the hospital who were killed due to shelling of the hospital premises?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I drove up to the orthopaedic clinic, to the entrance to that clinic, and I really didn't see that plaque. I was given to the orthopaedic clinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know that there is such a plaque there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of that. I didn't see it. And the colleagues with me didn't speak to me about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, you used the word "plaque," and I used the word "memorial". How do you know it was a plaque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said plaque by chance, it is called a plaque or a memorial, you know, whenever you have a memorial you have a plaque with the name on it. So when we talk about memorials we also mention plaques. These terms are synonymous for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, you said during the times you were working at the hospital you were in charge of admissions of patients?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you perhaps give an average or average estimate of how many patients were admitted to the hospital during the period May 1992 to January 1994? Perhaps an approximate figure.
