utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were days when there wasn't a single wounded person. I was responsible for them. I wasn't responsible for other patients. But there were days when 100 wounded would be admitted, even over 100, and this includes those who were slightly wounded and those who were seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My question, sir, to you is whether you could give an approximate figure of the number of admissions, wounded patients who were admitted to the Kosevo Hospital? I am talking about the total amount during the period May 1992 to January 1994, the time you were there, and I am referring to the period of conflict.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there, I think the number was between 3 and 4.000, but this is a very rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to perhaps -- I withdraw that. Can you give an approximate figure of about how many civilians, wounded civilians, were admitted during this period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is a very rough estimate, I think 75 or 80 per cent were soldiers and the remainder, 20 or 23 per cent were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I asked you for the figures. Or how did you conclude that 70 or 75 per cent of the admissions were soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when we included -- when we took away the old people and children and people who weren't wearing uniforms, when we took that number away from the number of the soldiers, we were left with the figure for the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is true but to give a percentage you would have to have the numbers. Did you have the opportunity to make a survey or assess how many wounded civilians and how many wounded military personnel were admitted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A minute ago I said 3 to 4.000, and they were all listed in the same list, and we mentioned who was a civilian and who was -- we mentioned who was a civilian and who was a soldier. You can work out what the number of the soldiers were on the basis of the percentages given, 75 person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, your 24 minutes are over.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I could perhaps be given two more questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two more questions I will allow you, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, you stated in examination-in-chief that you saw armed individuals being admitted to the hospital, you said sometimes personnel in uniform as well as persons with arms were admitted to the hospital. And I am referring to transcript page number 13628.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, you're correct. There were people who were in civilian clothing wearing carrying weapons and we considered them to be soldiers. I considered them to be soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir is it your impression -- is it your position that injured, wounded people were admitted to the hospital still carrying arms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were weapons in each corner of the hospital. Most of the wounded people came with weapons on them. One such man -- one such man also ran after me so I ran away to the roof of the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, one more question as a follow up to that response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that is really the last question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When you said that wounded persons were admitted to the hospital with weapons on them, are you suggesting that they were carrying weapons, there were weapons placed on these persons, wounded people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were bearing weapons, and many had weapons on the hospital beds that they were lying on. Security was just unable to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That was my last question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Nieto-Navia has one or more questions to put to you, Mr. DP51.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Only one question and my question is: You said that you lived with a certain amount of fear. When you said that were you referring to a special fear because you were a Serb living within the BH population or a general fear as a normal person living in a place where a war was being held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two causes for my fear. Firstly, I could have been killed like anyone else in Sarajevo; and secondly, because I was a Serb and on the few occasions that I went into town, I always went with Muslim friends and they still visit me today. So there were two reasons for my fear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi always has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] I would just like to clarify something. Firstly, you said and I'll quote you so that there are no misunderstandings [In English] "It is possible to hear." [Interpretation] It is possible to hear a shell, it is possible to hear its trajectory because it has a sound which is similar to the sound of a plane. Is this also true for mortar shells?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For mortar shells? But there weren't any mortar shells. Mortar shells don't have such a range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am quoting you because you spoke about tank fire. You said you could hear the shell, in the air you could hear the sound. So my question is, did you yourself hear the sound of a mortar shell, for example, could you distinguish between the sound produced by a mortar shell and the sound produced by a tank shell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. I am not such an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. My second question concerns the following: When you were testifying you said that you could see the tank firing the first shell, and then you would flee. I'd like to know whether you fled because you were afraid that shells would hit the hospital or was it possible that -- was an exchange of fire possible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. We weren't afraid of the guns, the field guns in front of the hospital. Soldiers wouldn't make such mistakes, but we were afraid of the response from the other side because of small errors and because the trajectory was long, the hospital could be hit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I have understood you correctly, you were afraid of a possible reaction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my last question, could you tell me the name of -- could you tell me again about Juka Prazina's wife, what was her work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I said that a minute ago, she worked in an outpatient clinic in the town of Sarajevo before the war, and Juka, well, he was a freelance manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. I will interrupt you because we are running out of time. I thought she was a nurse.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a nurse in an outpatient clinic in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and she was wounded in the cheek, the joint?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in the cheek.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you say when this incident took place, was it while she had -- while she was performing her duties or was she somewhere else or at home or perhaps you don't know. Could you provide us with more information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't. I can't. I saw her when she was lying in the clinic, when she spent five or six days in the clinic, and where she was wounded and what the conditions were I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was this wound caused by a bullet, a shell fragment, what was the cause of the wound, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP51 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a fragment of a projectile, an explosive device, that's what caused the wound, a fragment of a projectile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since I have no further questions to you, this concludes your testimony in this court. I can imagine that you are relieved that you will be able to return. I wanted to thank you very much not only for coming, as I ask most of them, but even for -- just if you have one second. Could you please put your earphones on. I wanted to thank you not just for coming, but even for coming twice, which is quite unusual. Thank you very much for answering all the questions of the parties and the questions of the bench. And I hope that you will again have a safe journey home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good-bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please guide us through the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1757 under seal, pseudonym sheet; Exhibit D1758 under seal, map marked by witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both documents are admitted into evidence since there are no objections, 1757 under seal. Yes. I am making a mistake, the map also under seal, 1758. I take it -- yes. I made a mistake. Both documents are admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber, although usually using the time up to the very last minute, considers it perhaps better not to start the examination of the next witness. If there would be any other issue to be raised, we have nine minutes left, so it could be done at this very moment. But I see that none of the parties has any issue. Yes, Mr. Ierace. Yes, I wondered whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I can hardly let the opportunity to go past, Mr. President, but I think this is relatively uncontentious. Can I simply confirm the identity of the next witness, perhaps in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 6.41 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 9th day of December, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
